**Version 1.0.0** · requires FOS Essentials Core 1.1.0 or later

A lighting, FX and cue console for your world. Requires **FOS Essentials Core 1.1.0**.

You bring the lights, the animations and the effects. This pack holds the **show**: which
look is on, at what level, and how long it takes to get there — the same for everyone in
the room, latecomers included.

---

## The idea in one picture

```
Console  ──►  Show Director  ──►  Show Light      → your Light
(buttons,     (the show, and     Show Material   → your neon
 faders)       the only thing    Show Particles  → your smoke, your confetti
               on the network)   Show Toggle     → your effects
                                 Show Animator   → your animations
                                 Show Relay      → ProTV, AudioLink, your scripts
```

Nothing on the right ever talks to anything on the left. Add a light without touching the
console; rebuild the console without touching a single light.

---

## Components

| Component | Role |
|---|---|
| `FOSShowDirector` | Holds the show. One per world. **Alone on its GameObject.** |
| `FOSShowLight` | Drives one Light: an intensity and a colour per cue. |
| `FOSShowToggle` | Switches a group of objects on or off per cue. Your FX go here. |
| `FOSShowAnimator` | Plays one of your animations per cue, in phase for everyone. |
| `FOSShowParticles` | Emits or fires one shot per cue. Smoke, confetti, sparks. |
| `FOSShowMaterial` | Recolours an emissive surface per cue. Neon, LED, screens. |
| `FOSShowRelay` | Sends a named event to any Udon behaviour on a cue. |
| `FOSShowButton` | A console key: call a cue, black out, replay. Labels and lights itself. |
| `FOSShowSlider` | A console fader: master level, or fade time. |
| `FOSShowReadout` | Writes the show's state into TextMeshPro labels. |

Menu: `Add Component > FOS Essentials > Show Control > ...`

---

## Setup

1. Drop **FOS Show Console** into your scene, from the pack's `Prefabs` folder or from
   `FOS Essentials > Show Control`. It brings the director with it: sixteen keys, a master
   fader, a fade fader, blackout and replay, already wired.
2. On each of your lights, add a **Show Light** and drag the director into it. The
   director sits inside the console prefab, under `Show Director`.
3. On an empty object holding your effects, add a **Show Toggle** and drag the director in.
4. Light your scene by hand until cue 0 looks right. On the director, open the **cue
   sheet**, name the line, and press **Store**.
5. Change the lighting, store it into cue 1. Repeat for as many looks as you need.
6. Press **Label the console keys** on the director. A key carries its cue's number and
   name from the cue sheet, so you type a name once and not twice.

That is the whole setup. Everything past this point is your venue, not the pack.

**One director per world.** The console prefab contains one; dropping the prefab twice
gives you two shows that ignore each other. To drive the same show from a second surface,
copy the console and point its keys at the first director.

**Building your own console instead** — a modelled desk, a wall panel, a handheld remote —
is a matter of putting `FOSShowButton` and `FOSShowSlider` on your own objects and pointing
them at the director. The manual walks through it, including the physical-desk case: a key
answers `Interact()` as well as a UI Button, so the same component works on a modelled key
with a collider.

**Recall** puts the scene back the way a stored cue had it, so you can go on editing a
look you already recorded.

Every field on a **Show Readout** is optional, so put one wherever the console displays
something: one in the header showing the cue number and name, another under the faders
showing their figures. An operator who did not press the key still needs to know where
the show is.

---

## The cue sheet is the point

Nobody types sixteen intensities by hand, and nobody gets a good look that way. So the
pack works like a real lighting desk: you build the look in the scene, then **record** it.

One consequence to know about: **a cue is a number, not a content.** The director only
ever sends "go to cue 4, in 2 seconds" over the network, and each node holds its own
table of values. That is why a hundred lights cost exactly the same bandwidth as one, and
why a node added later stays dark on the cues it never knew — press **Store** again, or
use the **resize** button the inspector offers you.

---

## Your animations, in phase

A `Show Animator` plays one of your animator states per cue. It knows nothing about what
it plays — you write the state or trigger name, your controller does the rest.

Each client plays that animation on its own machine, so a looping one would drift: two
players start it a moment apart, and somebody arriving later restarts it from zero. Tick
**align to the cue** and fill in **loop seconds**, and the animation resumes where it
should be by now instead of restarting — computed from the server clock the director
shares, without a single byte on the wire.

**A cue with an empty line does one of two things, and you choose which.** *Carry on* lets
the running animation continue — right for a set piece that spans several looks. *Freeze*
stops it where it stands, until a later cue names a state again — right for a moving head
that has no business sweeping any more. Freezing holds the pose rather than snapping back
to the start.

If you would rather control what "stopped" looks like, add an `Idle` state to your own
controller and name it on those cues. That works whichever option you picked.

## The FX, and which node to reach for

| You want | Node | Why that one |
|---|---|---|
| Neon or LED that changes colour | `Show Material` | costs almost nothing to draw, and carries a whole look on its own |
| Smoke, fog, snow | `Show Particles`, continuous | stops emitting and lets what is airborne drift away |
| Confetti, pyro, a spark hit | `Show Particles`, burst | one shot as the cue comes up, fired again by **Replay** |
| A laser rig, a prop, a banner | `Show Toggle` | on or off, nothing in between |
| Anything that moves | `Show Animator` | your animation, your controller |

A `Show Material` writes through a property block, so it never touches your material
asset and ten objects sharing one material can each show a different colour.

**The dark-neon trap:** on the Standard shader, writing `_EmissionColor` does nothing
while the material's **Emission** checkbox is off. That checkbox compiles a shader
keyword, and no code can switch it back on. Tick it once — a black emission colour is
fine — and the pack takes it from there.

---

## What crosses the network, and what does not

| | |
|---|---|
| Synced | the cue number, the trigger count, the master, the blackout, the fade time, and the server time the cue started — about a dozen bytes, on the director alone |
| Not synced | every node. A hundred lights cost exactly what one costs |
| Rebuilt on join | everything. A latecomer reads the director's state and lands mid-show, mid-fade-free, mid-animation |

Anybody may drive the console: pressing a key takes ownership of the director. Restricting
that to a crew is what **FOS Access** and **FOS Show Control Pro** are for.

Sending is throttled: a fader dragged across its travel produces one network update every
fifth of a second, not fifty. What you see locally is never delayed — only the wire is
spared.

---

## ProTV, AudioLink, and anything else

`FOSShowRelay` sends an event name. That is deliberately all it does: a hard reference to
ProTV would stop this pack from compiling for everyone who does not own it.

- Point a relay at your ProTV player, write the event you want on the cue's row, and tick
  **relay from the operator only** — otherwise every client in the room fights for
  ownership of the video player.
- The same relay drives AudioLink, USharpVideo, or a behaviour you wrote yourself.

Ready-made bridges — driving ProTV by track, making lights breathe with AudioLink's
frequency bands — are what **FOS Show Control Pro** adds.

---

## Quest

- One `Update` in the whole system, on the director, and it exits on the first line when
  nothing is fading. Your lights have none.
- A `Show Light` switches its Light component off once it reaches zero. A realtime light
  at zero intensity still costs; a disabled one does not.
- Realtime lights remain expensive on Quest whatever we do. Baked lighting plus a few
  realtime accents will always beat twenty realtime spots.

---

## Two silent traps the inspector watches for you

- **The director must be alone on its GameObject.** VRChat applies one single sync mode
  per object, taken from the last behaviour on it: a node dropped next to the director
  would quietly break the whole show.
- **A toggle must never target its own object.** A disabled object stops running its Udon
  behaviour, so it would never receive the cue meant to bring it back.

---

## What Pro adds

Sequencer and timeline, chases and strobes (computed from network time, so they cost
nothing), colour presets, ready-made ProTV and AudioLink bridges, console access
restricted by role through **FOS Access**, and a **FOS Tablet System** panel.
